title: The Case of the Missing Eyepiece

passage.title: The Case of the Missing Eyepiece
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
At five o'clock on Friday, the sky above Pinecrest School was turning a clear, deep blue. In thirty minutes, families would gather on the soccer field for the fifth-grade astronomy night. Jonah stood in the lab and opened the wood case for the school's big brass scope. His smile faded as soon as he lifted the soft lid. The long brass tube was there, but the small magnifying lens was gone from its slot. Without that curved glass piece, Saturn's rings would look like a blurry smudge.

Across the room, Jonah's friend Tessa was taping star charts onto boards. When Jonah showed her the empty slot, Tessa wanted to run down the hall and search the lost-and-found bin right away. Jonah shook his head and asked her to wait a second. Running around the school in a rush would waste their last half hour. Instead, he looked closely at the lab table. Mr. Patel's class had cleaned the glass there after lunch.

A folded square of white lens paper lay beside an empty tray of microscope slides. On the smooth black table, a faint ring of white chalk dust marked where a small round cylinder had rested. Jonah knew that the art club had shared the lab at three o'clock. They had drawn chalk posters of the moon and stars. If the eyepiece had been sitting on the table during art club, someone must have moved it to keep chalk dust off the glass.

Jonah and Tessa walked over to the drying rack near the back sink where the moon art hung. Right beside the rack stood a row of tall glass beakers turned upside down on a clean towel. The missing brass eyepiece, tucked safely beneath an overturned glass beaker to shield the lens from pastel dust, was quickly spotted by Jonah near the window. A note on the glass read, "Kept clean for tonight!" in the art teacher's neat script.

Tessa let out a big sigh of relief. Jonah slid the brass lens back into the tube and turned the small screw tight. Together, they carried the stand out the doors toward the dark field just as the first parents walked up. Tessa said that her plan to dig through the coat bin in the office would have made them late. By slowing down and reading the clues in the room, Jonah had saved the clearest view in the solar system.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"The missing brass eyepiece, tucked safely beneath an overturned glass beaker to shield the lens from pastel dust, was quickly spotted by Jonah near the window."

Based on the structure of the sentence, who or what spotted the missing brass eyepiece?

options.text: The overturned glass beaker spotted the pastel dust on the window.
options.childFeedback: A glass beaker does not have eyes to spot anything! The overturned beaker was just covering the brass lens to keep chalk dust off it.

options.text: The missing brass eyepiece spotted Jonah beside the drying rack.
options.childFeedback: This flips the action backward! The brass eyepiece is an object that was found—Jonah is the person who spotted it.

options.text: Jonah spotted the missing brass eyepiece near the window.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, the phrase 'by Jonah' right after 'was quickly spotted' shows that Jonah is the person who spotted the missing brass eyepiece near the window.

options.text: The art teacher spotted the telescope on the soccer field.
options.childFeedback: The art teacher left a helpful note on the glass beaker earlier, and the telescope was not carried out to the soccer field until Paragraph 5.

questions.provingSentenceText: The missing brass eyepiece, tucked safely beneath an overturned glass beaker to shield the lens from pastel dust, was quickly spotted by Jonah near the window.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, the phrase 'by Jonah' right after 'was quickly spotted' shows that Jonah is the person who spotted the missing brass eyepiece near the window.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice sentence, 'The missing brass eyepiece' receives the action, while the prepositional phrase 'by Jonah' identifies Jonah as the actor who spotted it.
questions.retryHint: Look at the words 'was quickly spotted by Jonah' in Paragraph 4 to see who did the spotting.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"The missing brass eyepiece, tucked safely beneath an overturned glass beaker to shield the lens from pastel dust, was quickly spotted by Jonah near the window."

What does the word shield mean as it is used in Paragraph 4?

options.text: To protect something by covering it from harm or dirt
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'shield' means to protect something by covering it from harm or dirt, because the overturned glass beaker kept chalk dust off the clean lens.

options.text: To hide an object so nobody can ever find it
options.childFeedback: The art teacher was not trying to hide the lens forever—she placed a clear glass beaker over it with a note saying 'Kept clean for tonight!'

options.text: To polish glass with a dry paper towel
options.childFeedback: White lens paper sat on the lab table in Paragraph 3, but in Paragraph 4 the overturned glass beaker was used to cover and protect the lens.

options.text: To carry heavy science tools out to a dark field
options.childFeedback: Jonah and Tessa carry the telescope stand out to the dark field in Paragraph 5, whereas 'shield' in Paragraph 4 describes what the glass beaker did on the counter.

questions.provingSentenceText: The missing brass eyepiece, tucked safely beneath an overturned glass beaker to shield the lens from pastel dust, was quickly spotted by Jonah near the window.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'shield' means to protect something by covering it from harm or dirt, because the overturned glass beaker kept chalk dust off the clean lens.
questions.parentExplanation: The context clues 'tucked safely beneath an overturned glass beaker' and 'Kept clean for tonight!' show that 'shield' means to protect from dirt or harm.
questions.retryHint: Look at the note 'Kept clean for tonight!' in Paragraph 4 to see why the glass beaker was placed over the lens.

questions.prompt: How do Jonah and Tessa respond differently when they first discover that the telescope eyepiece is missing in Paragraph 2?

options.text: Both students immediately run down the hallway to ask Mr. Patel where he put the microscope slides.
options.childFeedback: Neither student runs to ask Mr. Patel; Jonah stays in the lab and examines the table where Mr. Patel's class had cleaned the glass.

options.text: Jonah wants to cancel astronomy night right away, while Tessa offers to draw a paper lens instead.
options.childFeedback: You cannot use a paper drawing as a magnifying telescope lens, and neither student suggests canceling astronomy night.

options.text: Tessa blames the art teacher for breaking the glass, while Jonah hides the empty wooden case.
options.childFeedback: Neither student blames the art teacher or hides the case; in fact, the art teacher is the one who protected the lens under a clean beaker.

options.text: Tessa wants to rush to the lost-and-found bin, while Jonah stays calm and examines the lab table for clues.

questions.prompt: Why is the detail about the ring of white chalk dust in Paragraph 3 important to the plot of the mystery?

options.text: It proves that Mr. Patel's third-period class forgot to clean the telescope after lunch.
options.childFeedback: The folded lens paper on the table shows Mr. Patel's class did clean the glass after lunch; the chalk dust came from the three o'clock art club.

options.text: It helps Jonah realize that someone moved the lens during art club to protect it from pastel dust.
options.childFeedback: Spotting the faint ring of white chalk dust on the black table in Paragraph 3 helps Jonah figure out that someone moved the eyepiece during art club to keep chalk dust off the glass.

options.text: It shows that the brass eyepiece was permanently ruined by wet paint and glue.
options.childFeedback: The brass eyepiece was not ruined at all—the art teacher tucked it safely under a glass beaker so it stayed clean for astronomy night.

options.text: It explains why Saturn's rings look like a circle of white dust in outer space.
options.childFeedback: The white ring on the black lab table was left by chalk pastels from art club, not a science lesson about what Saturn's rings are made of.

questions.provingSentenceText: If the eyepiece had been sitting on the table during art club, someone must have moved it to keep chalk dust off the glass.
questions.childTip: Spotting the faint ring of white chalk dust on the black table in Paragraph 3 helps Jonah figure out that someone moved the eyepiece during art club to keep chalk dust off the glass.
questions.parentExplanation: The ring of chalk dust on the table is the key clue in Paragraph 3 that connects the cleaned lens to the afternoon art club, leading Jonah to deduce that someone covered it nearby to protect it.
questions.retryHint: Read the last sentence of Paragraph 3 to see what Jonah figures out after noticing the ring of white chalk dust.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which statement best expresses the main lesson of the story?

options.text: Art clubs and science classes should never be allowed to share the same room at school.
options.childFeedback: The art teacher actually helped save astronomy night by keeping the lens clean under a beaker, so sharing the room was not the problem.

options.text: School lost-and-found bins are always the best place to look for missing science equipment.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 5, Tessa admits that digging through the coat bin in the office would have wasted time and made them late.

options.text: Slowing down to observe clues carefully solves problems faster than rushing around in a panic.
options.childFeedback: The story shows that by staying calm and observing the clues in the room instead of rushing to the office lost-and-found bin, Jonah found the lens in time for astronomy night.

options.text: Telescopes work just as well without an eyepiece lens if the night sky is clear enough.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 states the exact opposite: without that curved magnifying lens, Saturn's rings would look like a blurry smudge.

questions.provingSentenceText: By slowing down and reading the clues in the room, Jonah had saved the clearest view in the solar system.
questions.childTip: The story shows that by staying calm and observing the clues in the room instead of rushing to the office lost-and-found bin, Jonah found the lens in time for astronomy night.
questions.parentExplanation: The central lesson of the story is that pausing to observe clues and think logically succeeds where panicking and rushing around would have wasted time.
questions.retryHint: Look at the last two sentences of Paragraph 5 to see what Tessa admits and how Jonah solved the problem in time.
